cls: Antimuscarinic (quaternary ammonium) antispasmodic - smooth muscle relaxant
pharm: Quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic and direct smooth muscle relaxant that reduces gastrointestinal smooth muscle spasm and tone, relieving abdominal pain and cramping.
quick: 50 mg orally three times daily (commonly before meals)
Often taken before meals for spasmodic abdominal pain
Avoid unless clearly needed; limited data
Caution; antimuscarinics may reduce milk and pass into milk
May add to drowsiness; use caution
Antimuscarinic effects (dry mouth, vision, urinary retention); symptom relief
summary: Cimetropium bromide is a quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic antispasmodic with direct smooth-muscle-relaxant activity, derived from scopolamine. It is used to relieve smooth muscle spasm of the gastrointestinal tract, including the pain of irritable bowel syndrome and other spasmodic abdominal conditions, and is sometimes used to reduce spasm during endoscopy. Because it is a quaternary compound, it penetrates the central nervous system poorly, so central anticholinergic effects are limited; peripheral antimuscarinic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, tachycardia) can still occur. It is not FDA-approved (see pearls); guidance is based on European/other national product information.
indications: Symptomatic relief of smooth muscle spasm of the gastrointestinal tract, including spasmodic abdominal pain
Relief of pain associated with irritable bowel syndrome and functional gastrointestinal spasm
Reduction of gastrointestinal smooth muscle spasm during diagnostic procedures (e.g., endoscopy) - per local practice

dosage.n: Commonly taken before meals; per product label

dosage.d: Per product label for procedural/acute use
Use the lowest effective dose for symptom control

admin: Take oral doses as directed, commonly before meals for spasmodic pain
Parenteral forms (where available) are administered by a clinician for acute or procedural spasm
Use the lowest effective dose and review the need for continued treatment
Counsel on antimuscarinic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision) and avoiding driving if vision is affected
moa: Cimetropium bromide is a semisynthetic quaternary ammonium derivative of scopolamine. It acts as a competitive antagonist at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors on gastrointestinal smooth muscle, blocking acetylcholine-mediated contraction, and also has a direct (musculotropic) relaxant effect on smooth muscle. Together these reduce smooth muscle tone and spasm in the gut, relieving cramping pain. Because the quaternary nitrogen makes the molecule poorly lipid-soluble, it does not readily cross the blood-brain barrier, so central anticholinergic effects are minimal compared with tertiary amine antimuscarinics.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to cimetropium bromide or other antimuscarinics
Urinary retention or significant bladder outflow obstruction (e.g., prostatic hypertrophy)
Gastrointestinal obstruction, paralytic ileus, or severe ulcerative colitis/toxic megacolon
Obstructive disease of the gastrointestinal or urinary tract
relative: Fever or high ambient temperature (reduced sweating)
monitor: Peripheral antimuscarinic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, tachycardia)
Symptom relief and continued need for therapy

preg: There are limited data on cimetropium bromide in pregnancy. Avoid use unless clearly needed and the potential benefit outweighs the risk, in line with the product information.
lact: Antimuscarinic agents may reduce milk production and can pass into breast milk. Use with caution during breastfeeding; weigh benefit against potential infant exposure per the product information.
renal: There is limited information on use in renal impairment; use with caution.
hepatic: There is limited information on use in hepatic impairment; use with caution.

major: Other anticholinergic/antimuscarinic drugs (atropine, antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, antipsychotics, antiparkinsonian agents) - additive antimuscarinic effects (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, confusion)
moderate: Prokinetic agents (e.g., metoclopramide, domperidone) - antagonistic effects on gastrointestinal motility
Drugs slowing gastric emptying - may alter absorption of co-administered drugs
Class IA/III antiarrhythmics and other drugs affecting heart rate - additive effects on cardiac rhythm
interactions.food: Often taken before meals for spasmodic pain; food does not markedly alter its antispasmodic action.
interactions.alcohol: May add to drowsiness; use caution with alcohol.
interactions.diagnostics: Antimuscarinic activity can affect gastrointestinal motility and may influence procedures or motility studies.

rare: Confusion (uncommon owing to poor CNS penetration)

monitoring: Watch for antimuscarinic adverse effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, tachycardia)
Symptom relief and ongoing need for treatment
Intraocular pressure in patients at risk of glaucoma
Bowel and bladder function, especially in the elderly
counsel: Take as directed, usually before meals, to relieve cramping abdominal pain
This medicine can cause dry mouth, blurred vision, and constipation - sip water and report bothersome effects
Do not drive or operate machinery if your vision is blurred or you feel dizzy
Tell your doctor if you have glaucoma, trouble passing urine, an enlarged prostate, or heart rhythm problems
Avoid taking it with other 'drying' (anticholinergic) medicines unless advised
pk: Antispasmodic effect within about 30-60 minutes of an oral dose
Peak effect within a few hours; absorption is limited (quaternary compound)
Several hours, consistent with three-times-daily dosing
Store at controlled room temperature; protect from moisture per the product label
pearls: Not FDA-approved; used in Europe/other regions - guidance based on EMA/national SmPC and product information
Quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic (scopolamine derivative) - poor CNS penetration means central anticholinergic effects are minimal
Useful for IBS-type cramping and to reduce GI spasm during endoscopy
Contraindicated in narrow-angle glaucoma, urinary retention/prostatic obstruction, GI obstruction, and myasthenia gravis
Watch for peripheral antimuscarinic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, tachycardia)
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at once.
overdose: Overdose produces exaggerated antimuscarinic effects: dry mouth, dilated pupils and blurred vision, flushing, hot dry skin, urinary retention, tachycardia, agitation, and, with large doses, hyperthermia and (less likely due to poor CNS penetration) central excitation. Management is supportive: ensure airway and hydration, control hyperthermia, catheterize for urinary retention if needed, and use activated charcoal if appropriate. In severe peripheral antimuscarinic toxicity, a cholinesterase inhibitor (e.g., physostigmine/neostigmine) may be considered under specialist guidance, with cardiac monitoring.
